sheet.howExamined: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. A trigonometric graph has opened an early question in most papers: Summer 2018 Q3(a) (cosine from 0° to 360°, 2 marks), Summer 2019 Q4(a) (cosine from −90° to 360°), Summer 2022 Q4(a) (sine from −360° to 0°, 1), Summer 2023 Q3(a) (cosine from −180° to 180°, 2) and Summer 2025 Q2(a) (complete the tangent graph from −90° to 270°, 1). The axes are printed for you and the wording is Sketch the graph of or Complete the graph of, with the range written underneath. The marks are for the shape and for the scale or key points. The part that follows usually solves an equation on the same curve for 2 or 3 marks, and the sketch is the check on its angles.
traps: Joining the key points with straight lines instead of one smooth curve, which earns the points and loses the shape (Summer 2018 FM1 Q3, Summer 2019 FM1 Q4)
Leaving the axes without a scale, so the values mean nothing (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4, Summer 2023 FM1 Q3)
Starting a cosine sketch at the origin, which is the sine curve drawn by mistake
Leaving the asymptotes off a tangent sketch, or drawing them at 180° (Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)
Letting the tangent curve touch or cross an asymptote (Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)
Running off the bottom of the grid instead of turning at the minimum (Summer 2023 FM1 Q3)
Giving 360° as the period of tan x, or 180° as the period of sin x
Changing the sign when using symmetry, which reflects the curve in the x-axis instead of sideways
Stopping at the calculator's angle when the drawn line clearly cuts the curve twice (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4)
A curve drawn upside down (Summer 2022 FM1 Q4)
Too few angles marked along the x-axis (Summer 2019 FM1 Q4)
A sine or cosine shape drawn where the tangent was asked (Summer 2025 FM1 Q2)

noteBlocks.lede: Stand a wheel on its edge, mark one spoke and turn it: the height of the mark rises and falls forever. Drawn against the angle, that height is the sine curve. Cosine is the same wave started at the top, and tangent is a third shape that repeats twice as often.
can: Sketch y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x over a given range, with the key points and a scale
Use the period, and tangent's asymptotes, to carry a sketch to any range on the paper
Count and read solutions off a curve, and use its symmetry to turn one angle into another

noteBlocks.text: The sine curve: a wheel's height

noteBlocks.md: Stand a wheel on its edge, mark one spoke and turn it. Plot the height of the mark against the angle turned and you get the **sine curve**. It starts at 0, rises to 1 at $90^\circ$, is back to 0 at $180^\circ$, falls to $-1$ at $270^\circ$ and returns to 0 at $360^\circ$.

noteBlocks.md: A sketch earns two marks: one for the shape and one for the scale or the key points. So write 90, 180, 270 and 360 along the bottom and 1 and −1 up the side, then join the points with one smooth curve, rounded at the top and at the bottom.

steps.decision: A calculator in degrees gives the value every 90°: these are the key points.
The scale is a mark of its own: angles along the bottom, 1 and −1 up the side.

steps.working: Join them with one smooth curve, rounded at $(90, 1)$ and $(270, -1)$
steps.decision: Turning points are curves, never corners: straight sides cost the shape mark.

noteBlocks.prompt: Without a calculator, is $\sin 250^\circ$ positive or negative?
options: Negative
Positive
Zero
noteBlocks.explain: As steps 2 and 3 of See it: after crossing the axis at $180^\circ$ the sine curve dips to its lowest point and only returns to 0 at the end of the turn. $250^\circ$ is in that dip, so its value is below zero.

twin.prompt: Without a calculator, is $\sin 160^\circ$ positive or negative?
options: Positive
Negative
Zero
twin.explain: Up to $180^\circ$ the whole first arch is above the axis, even where it is falling, so the value is above zero.

optionNotes.why: Falling is not negative: the whole first arch, up to 180°, stays above the axis.
Zero is at 180°; at 160° the curve has not yet come down to the axis.
Positive is the first arch, 0° to 180°; 250° is past 180°, where the curve has dipped below the axis.
Sine is zero only at 0°, 180° and 360°; at 250° the curve is below the axis.

noteBlocks.text: Cosine: the same wave, started high

noteBlocks.md: On the wheel, $\sin x$ is how far up the mark is and $\cos x$ is how far across. At $0^\circ$ the spoke points straight across, so cosine starts at its greatest value, 1. The **cosine curve** is the sine curve slid $90^\circ$ to the left: the same shape and height, a different start.

noteBlocks.caption: The cosine curve from 0° to 360°: the sine wave started at its top.

noteBlocks.title: Why both stay between −1 and 1
noteBlocks.md: The spoke has length 1, so the mark is never more than 1 above, below, left or right of the centre. That is why the greatest value of sine and cosine is 1 and the least is −1, on every range.

noteBlocks.stem: Find the key points for a sketch of $y = \cos x$ for $-90^\circ \le x \le 270^\circ$.

steps.decision: The calculator again, every 90° from the start of the range: an angle below zero is a turn the other way.
Half a turn points the spoke straight back: as far across as it goes, the other way.
The highest point sits on the y-axis: a cosine sketch never starts at the origin.

noteBlocks.prompt: For how many values of $x$ in $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$ is $\cos x = 0$?
noteBlocks.explain: As step 3 of See it: the cosine curve crosses the axis a quarter turn either side of its lowest point, at $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$. Its ends, $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, are at the top, so there are two values.

twin.prompt: For how many values of $x$ in $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$ is $\cos x = -1$?
twin.explain: Only at $180^\circ$, the single lowest point of the cosine curve in that range.

noteBlocks.md: One full turn brings the spoke back to where it started, so sine and cosine repeat every $360^\circ$: that is their **period**. It is how a sketch reaches any range on the paper: whatever a curve does from $0^\circ$ to $360^\circ$, it also does from $-360^\circ$ to $0^\circ$.

noteBlocks.alt: The graph of y = sin x from −360° to 360°: the same wave twice, the stretch from 0° to 360° shaded as one period.
noteBlocks.caption: From −360° to 360° the sine wave runs twice: each 360° stretch is one period.

noteBlocks.stem: Find the key points for a sketch of $y = \sin x$ for $-360^\circ \le x \le 0^\circ$.

steps.working: Take $360$ from each $x$ of the key points from $0^\circ$ to $360^\circ$
steps.decision: The period is 360°, so this range holds the same wave slid back one period.
Each x is 360 less; each height is unchanged.
One value on the calculator confirms the slide.

noteBlocks.prompt: Given that $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$, write down the value of $\sin(-330^\circ)$.
noteBlocks.explain: As step 1 of See it, slide by one period: $-330 + 360 = 30$, so $-330^\circ$ sits at the same place on the wave as $30^\circ$ and the value is the same.

twin.prompt: Given that $\sin 45^\circ = 0.71$, write down the value of $\sin(-315^\circ)$.
twin.explain: $-315 + 360 = 45$: one period apart, so the same height.

noteBlocks.md: $\tan x$ is $\sin x$ divided by $\cos x$. Where $\cos x = 0$, at $90^\circ$, $270^\circ$ and every $180^\circ$ from them, the division has no answer, so the curve has no value there. It climbs or falls steeply beside a dashed vertical line called an **asymptote**.

noteBlocks.alt: The graph of y = tan x from −360° to 0°: dashed asymptotes at −270° and −90°, a rising branch between each pair of them, crossing the axis at −360°, −180° and 0°.
noteBlocks.caption: y = tan x from −360° to 0°: dashed asymptotes at −270° and −90°, one rising branch between each.

noteBlocks.md: Each branch rises from bottom left to top right through a crossing of the axis, and the pattern repeats every $180^\circ$: tangent's period is half that of the other two curves.

steps.decision: Where cos x = 0 in this range: 90° and 270° with 360 taken off.
tan x = 0 where sin x = 0, every 180°.

steps.working: One rising branch between each pair of dashed lines, never reaching them
steps.decision: Each branch climbs steeply towards a line, and the next one starts far below it on its other side.

noteBlocks.prompt: On a sketch of $y = \tan x$, what must the curve do as it nears a dashed asymptote?
options: It gets closer and closer without ever touching
It touches the line and turns back
It crosses the line at a steep angle
noteBlocks.answer: It gets closer and closer without ever touching
noteBlocks.explain: As step 3 of See it: at an asymptote $\cos x = 0$, so $\tan x$ has no value there and nothing on the curve can touch the line. A curve that meets or crosses one loses the mark.

twin.prompt: On a sketch of $y = \tan x$, where does the curve come from just to the right of an asymptote?
options: From far below the axis
From far above the axis
From the origin
twin.explain: Just left of an asymptote tan x is very large and positive; just right of it, very large and negative, so the next branch rises from far below.

optionNotes.why: The branch on the left climbs towards the line; the one on the right starts far below it.
The next branch crosses the axis 180° after the last crossing, not at the origin.

optionNotes.option: It touches the line and turns back
optionNotes.why: The curve has no point on the line: tan x has no value where cos x = 0.

optionNotes.option: It crosses the line at a steep angle
optionNotes.why: Crossing needs a value of tan x on the line itself, and there is none.

noteBlocks.md: To solve $\sin x = k$, $\cos x = k$ or $\tan x = k$ on a range, draw the horizontal line $y = k$ across the sketch. Each crossing is one solution, so the picture says how many to find and roughly where, before any calculator is touched (2022).

noteBlocks.alt: The graph of y = cos x from −360° to 360° with the dashed line y = 0.5 cutting it at four dotted points.
noteBlocks.caption: The line y = 0.5 cuts the cosine curve four times between −360° and 360°.

noteBlocks.stem: How many solutions has $\cos x = 0.5$ for $-360^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, and where are they?

steps.decision: Each crossing of the line and the curve is one solution.

steps.working: It cuts the curve twice in each $360^\circ$, so there are $4$ solutions
steps.decision: The range is two periods long, and each period gives two crossings.

steps.working: The calculator gives $60^\circ$; the sketch puts one more crossing in each of the other three arches
steps.decision: Read their places off the picture first; symmetry, next, makes them exact.

noteBlocks.prompt: How many solutions has $\tan x = 3$ for $-180^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$?
noteBlocks.explain: As steps 1 and 2 of See it: draw $y = 3$ across the tangent curve. The branch from $-180^\circ$ to $-90^\circ$ and the branch through $0^\circ$ each reach it once; the last branch only climbs to 0 at $180^\circ$.

twin.prompt: How many solutions has $\tan x = -1$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 270^\circ$?
twin.explain: The branch from $90^\circ$ to $270^\circ$ climbs from far below through $-1$ once, before $180^\circ$; the branch from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ stays above the axis.

noteBlocks.md: Each curve has a symmetry, so one angle gives a second with the same value. The first arch of sine is symmetrical about $x = 90^\circ$, so $\sin(180^\circ - x) = \sin x$. Cosine is symmetrical about $x = 180^\circ$, so $\cos(360^\circ - x) = \cos x$. Tangent simply repeats: $\tan(x + 180^\circ) = \tan x$.

items.stem:
Three quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new work, so answer from what you already know.
In a right-angled triangle, which ratio is $\sin \theta$?

options.feedback: That is the one. It is also why the sine curve never leaves the strip between -1 and 1: the opposite side can never be longer than the hypotenuse.
That is cosine. The two are easy to swap, and swapping them is what makes a sketch start in the wrong place.
That is tangent, which has no hypotenuse in it at all and so is not trapped between -1 and 1.

items.stem: A curve passes through the point where $x = 4$ and $y = -3$. How are those coordinates written?

options.feedback: Across first, then up or down. Every coordinate answer in this topic is written the same way.
The two numbers are right and they are the wrong way round. The x-value always comes first.
The order here is right. Brackets are how a pair is written, and a mark scheme asking for coordinates expects them.

items.stem: On a calculator set to degrees, what is $\cos 60^\circ$?
items.skill: Prerequisite: reading a trigonometric value in degrees

options.feedback: If your calculator gives something else, it is in radians, and every answer in Unit 1 would come out wrong.
The angle goes in and a ratio comes out, and for cosine that ratio is always between −1 and 1.
That is cos 60 in radians. Set the calculator to degrees before you start.

items.stem: Which curve passes through the point $(0, 1)$?
items.skill: Tell the sine and cosine curves apart

options.feedback: Cosine starts at its maximum, so it is at 1 when the angle is zero.
$\sin 0^\circ = 0$, so the sine curve starts at the origin and climbs from there.
$\tan 0^\circ = 0$ as well, so the tangent curve also starts on the axis.

items.stem: What is the period of $y = \tan x$?
items.skill: Recall the period of each curve

options.feedback: Half the period of the other two. One branch, then the same branch again.
$360^\circ$ is the period of sine and cosine. The tangent curve has already repeated once by then.
$90^\circ$ is the gap from a crossing to an asymptote, which is half a branch rather than a whole one.

items.stem: Where is the asymptote of $y = \tan x$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$?
items.skill: Place the asymptotes of the tangent curve

options.feedback: cos x = 0 at 90°, so tan x has no value there: the curve climbs beside the dashed line on one side and starts far below it on the other.
At 180° tan x = 0: the curve crosses the axis there. The asymptote is where cos x = 0, at 90°.
At 45° tan x = 1, a point on the curve. The asymptote is where cos x = 0, at 90°.

options.text: The points earn their mark; the shape mark is lost
options.feedback: Examiners have said this for several series running. Joining the points in one smooth pass is the whole difference.

options.text: Full marks, because the points are right
options.feedback: The shape is a separate mark, and straight sides between the turning points are what it is checking for.

findTheMistake.stem: Órlaith is told that $\sin 50^\circ = 0.77$ and asked for the value of $\sin 130^\circ$. Her working:
studentWorking: 130 is past the maximum, so the curve is on its way down
180 - 50 = 130, so the two angles are a pair
Going down means the value is negative
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Lines 1 and 2 are exactly right: $130^\circ$ does sit on the falling part of the arch, and it is the mirror image of $50^\circ$ in the line $x = 90^\circ$.
Line 3 confuses falling with negative. Between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ the whole arch sits above the axis, so every value there is positive however steeply the curve is dropping.
The curve only goes below the axis after $180^\circ$, and $130^\circ$ is comfortably short of that.
correction: The mirror line x = 90 leaves the height unchanged
findTheMistake.feedback: The method mark is safe: spotting the pair is the part that is worth thinking about, and Órlaith spotted it. Sketch the arch and mark both angles on it before writing the value down, and the sign settles itself.

findTheMistake.stem: Cormac was asked to use the graph of $y = \tan x$ to solve $\tan x = 2.5$ for $-180^\circ \le x \le 180^\circ$, to 1 decimal place. His working:
